text: Everything in this chapter so far has quietly assumed Discovery could actually reach the devices it's supposed to scan. This lesson covers what that actually takes in practice, starting with a requirement that has no exception at all: Discovery requires a MID Server, exactly as described in course 7.

ServiceNow's cloud instance can't directly reach IP addresses sitting on a customer's internal network. Course 7 covered exactly why: a MID Server, installed inside that network, makes outbound-only connections back to the instance, so nothing ever has to open inward through the firewall. Discovery is one of the specific jobs that architecture exists to enable — it's the MID Server, not the cloud instance, that actually sends the probes onto the network and relays results back. No MID Server reachable from the target range means no Discovery scan of that range, period.

A MID Server can only scan what it can actually reach. Whatever network segment it sits on needs real, permitted access through any firewalls between it and the target range, out to every address Discovery is meant to scan. If the MID Server's location can't route to the target subnet, or a firewall blocks the specific ports Discovery needs, the scan simply finds nothing there, no matter how correctly the Discovery Schedule itself is configured.

Reaching a device over the network is only half the job. Once Discovery finds something, running probes against it means authenticating to it, which is where course 7's Credential records come back in. A Linux server typically needs SSH credentials, a Windows server typically needs WMI credentials, and a network device might need SNMP credentials instead — one credential doesn't cover every device type, because the protocols themselves simply aren't interchangeable.

Without network access, Discovery's probes never get a response at all. Without the right credential, Discovery can usually still detect that something is there but can't authenticate to pull any detail, so the resulting CI ends up thin. Both requirements have to be in place together for Discovery to do the job Lesson 14 described. Next, Chapter 5 opens with a way to see whether Discovery is actually keeping the CMDB current: the CMDB Health Dashboard.
